I. Atanu Ghosh is a storyteller who explores the power of fairy tales to convey unhappy truths while holding up
the possibility of a happy outcome. His latest film, Aaro Ek Prithibi, is an original story fashioned from
contemporary lived-in experience. It is a post-colonial noir that uncovers a London that Bengali cinema and the
Bengali spectator have not explored. In Ghosh's noir-meets-fairy-tale, unrespectable people prove to be good
Samaritans, and he impels us to re-adjust our assessment of the bases of human bonding. Ghosh's stories are not
intended or contrived to look agentic. Women in his stories are not equated with greed for the good life but
instead are portrayed as they make their way through the plot of life.

Ghosh's art of storytelling is fluid, central to the cinematic flanerie that best describes his style. He is the quietly
watchful flaneur around the city and a little beyond, peering underneath the otherwise placid carpet of normality
with a gaze that is both piercing and humorous. His stories challenge us to rethink what we know about
ourselves and others, how our everyday differentiation between familiar and strange, known and alien, right and
wrong comes crashing down in crisis situations.
Ghosh's cinematography is a delicate visual construct, distinct in its use of light and darkness, indoors and
outdoors. If the change of light helps map the transitions, then the measured, restrained sound track, complete
with some deeply evocative lyrics, preserves the free flow.
Aaro Ek Prithibi pulls off a post-colonial noir by uncovering a London that Bengali cinema and the Bengali
spectator have not explored. Ghosh peels away all the glitz of the erstwhile capital of a far-flung Empire and
destabilizes the fantasies that fuel the desires that in turn sustain the NRI dream.

In the end, Aaro Ek Prithibi brings together essentially two worldviews: the one privileges truth-seeking as a
rational enterprise and the other foregrounds affective truth, with its less concrete but not necessarily shakier
moorings in faith, love, hope, compassion, and goodness.

Ghosh continues to find fresh stories and faces within the seemingly limited, unsensationally quotidian circle of
life that is urban, middle- and upper-middle-class Kolkata. Each new story inspires him to stretch his cinematic
art little by little to accommodate these ever-expanding worlds enlivened by his ever-expansive world-view.

II. In the world of technology, the race to be first is often seen as the key to success. After all, the first company
to bring a new technology to market is usually the one that shapes the product definitions and sets the standard
for everyone else to follow. However, in today's fast-paced business environment, being the first to market is no
longer enough. Instead, the biggest payoffs often go to companies that can successfully develop integrated
approaches for mass production and distribution.
A prime example of this phenomenon can be seen in the history of videocassette recorders (VCRs). In 1975,
producers of the Beta format were the first to bring VCRs to the commercial market. However, their rivals,


producers of the VHS (Video Home System) format, proved to be more successful at forming strategic alliances
with other producers and distributors to manufacture and market their VCR format. This allowed VHS to
quickly gain a dominant position in the global VCR market, despite Beta's substantial technological head start.

While Beta may have been the first to market, their reluctance to form strategic alliances eventually cost them
the competition. By seeking to maintain exclusive control over VCR distribution, they lost ground to VHS,
which was able to form alliances and secure a greater market share. Even though VHS was not technically
superior or cheaper than Beta, they quickly turned their slight early lead in sales into a dominant position.
One factor that contributed to VHS's success was their strategic alignments with producers of prerecorded tapes.
This reinforced their advantage and expanded their market share, as consumers perceived that prerecorded tapes
were more available in VHS format. By the end of the 1980s, Beta was no longer in production, and VHS had
become the dominant VCR format.

This example illustrates the importance of not only being the first to market but also having a comprehensive
strategy for mass production and distribution. Companies that are able to successfully integrate these elements
are more likely to come out on top in the long run. It's not enough to simply have a great product or technology;
it's essential to have a plan for how to get it into the hands of consumers.

Today's rapidly changing business environment means that companies must be agile and adaptable. The ability
to form strategic alliances, work collaboratively with other companies, and rapidly scale production and
distribution are all critical components of success. While being the first to market may offer a brief advantage,
it's ultimately the companies that can successfully develop and execute an integrated approach that will come
out on top.

III. Marcus Garvey, a Jamaican-born social activist, arrived in the United States in 1916, at a time when the
country was experiencing significant social upheaval. The return of African American soldiers from the First
World War in 1918 created a ripe environment for Garvey's message of unity, pride, and improved conditions
for African American communities. These soldiers, who had fought bravely for their country, returned home to a
United States that was as segregated as it had been before the war. This disconnect between expectations and
reality, according to anthropologist Anthony F. C. Wallace, can inspire a revitalization movement. In this case,
the movement was an organized, conscious effort to construct a culture that fulfilled longstanding expectations.

Garvey's message resonated deeply with African American communities across the country. He advocated for a
"back-to-Africa" movement, which aimed to promote black pride and self-sufficiency by creating an
independent black nation in Africa. This message was particularly appealing to those who were disillusioned
with the status quo and were looking for a new way forward. Garvey's ideas provided a sense of hope and
direction to those who had been marginalized and oppressed for generations.
Some scholars have argued that Garvey created the consciousness from which he built the largest revitalization
movement in African American history in the 1920s. However, others believe that Garvey merely gave voice to
a consciousness of identity, strength, and sense of history that already existed within the African American
community. Regardless of where one falls on this debate, there is no denying the impact that Garvey had on the
African American community.

Garvey's movement was unique in that it emphasized a sense of pride and self-sufficiency, rather than relying
on the goodwill of the white majority. This was a radical departure from the prevailing narrative of the time,
which suggested that African Americans should seek to assimilate into white society. Garvey's message was one
of empowerment, and it resonated deeply with those who had been marginalized and oppressed for generations.


Despite the many challenges that Garvey and his movement faced, including opposition from the government
and internal divisions, his ideas continued to spread. He founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association
(UNIA), which grew to become one of the largest and most influential organizations in African American
history. Through the UNIA, Garvey advocated for economic and political self-sufficiency, and his ideas inspired
generations of African American activists.

questions.stimulus:
IV. Choosing the perfect gift can be a difficult task. When in doubt, flowers and fruits are always acceptable
presents. Flowers are a proud assertion of beauty and a contrast to the somewhat stern countenance of ordinary
nature. They serve as a reminder that a ray of beauty outvalues all the utilities of the world. Fruits are the flower
of commodities and can have fantastic values attached to them.

For more common gifts, necessity makes pertinences and beauty every day. It is always satisfying to supply
basic necessities like bread and water. Necessity does everything well, and in our condition of universal
dependence, it is heroic to let the petitioner be the judge of his necessity and to give all that is asked, even if it is
inconvenient. However, fantastic desires should be left to the office of punishing them by others.

A gift should properly belong to the recipient's character and be easily associated with them in thought. Tokens
of compliment and love can often be barbarous. The only true gift is a portion of oneself. It restores society to a
point where a person's biography is conveyed in their gift. It is also an index of one's merit. The poet brings his
poem, the shepherd his lamb, the farmer his corn, the miner his gem, the sailor his coral and shells, the painter
his picture, and the girl a handkerchief of her own sewing.

Buying gifts can be a lifeless business. It is fit for kings and rich men who represent kings, but not for those
who wish to give a portion of themselves. While giving gifts can be difficult, receiving them can be even harder.
We are either glad or sorry at a gift, and both emotions are unbecoming. It is degrading to rejoice or grieve at a
gift. When a gift pleases us too much, we should be ashamed that the donor should read our hearts and see that
we love their commodity, not them.

The gift should be the flowing of the giver unto the recipient, correspondent to the recipient's flowing unto the
giver. When the waters are at level, then the goods pass from one to the other. Gratitude should not be expected,
as it is continually punished by the insensibility of the obliged person. Being served is a very onerous business,
and the debtor naturally wishes to give you a slap.

equality applied only within the limits of ordinary dealings. You cannot deal with someone, where both are free

But it seems clear to me that the ultima ratio, not only of rulers but of private persons, is force, and at the
bottom of all private relations, however tempered by sympathy and social feelings, is a justifiable self-
preference. If a man is on a plank in the deep sea that will only float one, and a stranger lays hold of it, he will
thrust him off if he can. When the state finds itself in a similar position, it does the same thing.

The considerations that answer the argument of equal rights also answer the objections to treating man as a
thing, and the like. If a man lives in society, he is liable to find himself so treated. The degree of civilization that
a people has reached, no doubt, is marked by their anxiety to do as they would be done by. However, the social
instincts have not yet grown to control our actions absolutely, even in anti-social situations. As the rules of law
are based upon a morality that is generally accepted, no rule founded on a theory of absolute unselfishness can
be laid down without a breach between law and working beliefs.

If it is true that the general principles of criminal and civil liability are the same, it will follow from that alone
that theory and fact agree in frequently punishing those who have been guilty of no moral wrong, and who
could not be condemned by any standard that did not avowedly disregard the personal peculiarities of the
individuals concerned. If punishment stood on the moral grounds that are proposed for it, the first thing to be
considered would be those limitations in the capacity for choosing rightly that arise from abnormal instincts,


want of education, lack of intelligence, and all the other defects which are most marked in the criminal classes.
The criminal law is not enacted or administered on that theory.

I. In a significant judgment boosting the interests of transparency, the Supreme Court held that the State cannot
claim absolute immunity from the disclosure of materials by merely claiming that they are related to national
security. Quashing the decision of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting to refuse renewal of the
telecast license for the Malayalam news channel MediaOne, the bench held that "concerns of national security
do not permit an absolute abrogation of the principles of natural justice".

The mere involvement of national security issues won't preclude the State's duty to act fairly: The Centre raised
the plea of "national security" to claim immunity for disclosure of the materials. Therefore, one of the issues
before the Supreme Court in the channel's appeal was whether national security was a complete exception to the
principles of natural justice. The Centre contended that decisions in Ex-Army men's Protection Services Private
Limited v. Union of India have held that the principles of natural justice have no application when national
security issues are involved.

The principle of Natural Justice is derived from the word ‘Jus Natural’ of Roman law and it is closely related to
Common law and moral principles but is not codified. The first one is audi alteram partem, i.e., “Hearing rule”
which states that the person or party who is affected by the decision made by the panel of expert members
should be given a fair opportunity to express his point of view to defend himself.
Secondly, nemo judex in causa sua, which is the “Bias rule” generally expresses that a panel of experts should
be biased-free while taking a decision. The decision should be made in a free and fair manner that can fulfil the
rule of natural justice. And thirdly, “Reasoned Decision” states that the order, decision or judgement of the court
is given by the Presiding authorities with valid and reasonable grounds.

II. A single-judge bench of the National Consumer Dispute Redressal Commission (NCDRC) comprising
presiding member Dr. Inderjit Singh, allowed a consumer complaint filed by the purchaser of a flat on account
of an inordinate delay caused by the developer. The Developer's contention, that the project could not be
completed on time since consumers defaulted in the payments, was rejected because as an experienced
developer, it was expected of him to be conscious of routine delays caused by the business exigencies. Thus, the
Commission reiterated that a dispute with the contractors over termination does not constitute force majeure.

‘Force Majeure’ is an event where a party to a contract of non-performance is excused or has frustrated the
contract rendering it impossible or impractical to perform. An Act of God includes all causes of an inevitable
accident to be occasioned by elementary forces of nature not connected with any agency of man or any other
cause directly or indirectly; on the other hand, the definition of Force Majeure is a much wider term that not
only includes the natural forces but also includes other causes which may not be related to nature and can be
connected to the human agency directly and indirectly, but on whom the humans involved in the accident don’t
have any control or the incident whose happening was inevitable and which cannot be controlled.

A force majeure clause, irrespective of its particular details, normally only applies to unanticipated situations
and beyond reasonable human forethought and expertise. It is indeed crucial to remember that when attempting
to depend on or exercise a force majeure clause, the impacted party is usually required to minimize the impacts
of the force majeure occurrence. Commercial reasonableness is the criteria for mitigation under a force majeure
situation. The impacted party must adhere to any contractual procedural obligations. These obligations involve


notifying the other party that the force majeure occurrence is interfering with the fulfilment of its contractual
obligations. This notice must be sent within the time range specified.

The party claiming the force majeure provision must show that the force majeure incident prohibited, hampered,
or postponed the performance of its contractual obligations. As a consequence of the force majeure incident, the
party must demonstrate that it was legally or practically impossible to execute its commitments.

presiding member Dr. Inderjit Singh, allowed a consumer complaint filed by the purchaser of a flat on account
of an inordinate delay caused by the developer. The Developer's contention, that the project could not be
completed on time since consumers defaulted in the payments, was rejected because as an experienced
developer, it was expected of him to be conscious of routine delays caused by the business exigencies. Thus, the
Commission reiterated that a dispute with the contractors over termination does not constitute force majeure.

‘Force Majeure’ is an event where a party to a contract of non-performance is excused or has frustrated the
contract rendering it impossible or impractical to perform. An Act of God includes all causes of an inevitable
accident to be occasioned by elementary forces of nature not connected with any agency of man or any other
cause directly or indirectly; on the other hand, the definition of Force Majeure is a much wider term that not
only includes the natural forces but also includes other causes which may not be related to nature and can be
connected to the human agency directly and indirectly, but on whom the humans involved in the accident don’t
have any control or the incident whose happening was inevitable and which cannot be controlled.

A force majeure clause, irrespective of its particular details, normally only applies to unanticipated situations
and beyond reasonable human forethought and expertise. It is indeed crucial to remember that when attempting
to depend on or exercise a force majeure clause, the impacted party is usually required to minimize the impacts
of the force majeure occurrence. Commercial reasonableness is the criteria for mitigation under a force majeure
situation. The impacted party must adhere to any contractual procedural obligations. These obligations involve


notifying the other party that the force majeure occurrence is interfering with the fulfilment of its contractual
obligations. This notice must be sent within the time range specified.

or postponed the performance of its contractual obligations. As a consequence of the force majeure incident, the
party must demonstrate that it was legally or practically impossible to execute its commitments.

questions.stimulus:
III. Right to Freedom to practice religion under Article 25 and 26 of Part III of the Indian Constitution is subject
to public morality, public order and public health. The rights under Articles 25 & 26 are not absolute or
unfettered but subject to legislation by the State limiting or regulating any activity, economic, financial, political
or secular which are associated with the religious behalf, faith, practice or custom and they are also subject to
social reform by suitable legislation. Article 25 gives individual right to freely profess, profess and practice their
religion while Article 26 gives every religious group a right to establish and maintain institutions for religious
and charitable purposes, manage its affairs, properties as per the law. Within the Constitution of India, these are
two impulses that may, at times, come into conflict with one another. The first impulse recognizes that India is a
pluralist and diverse nation, where groups and communities — whether religious or cultural — have always
played an important role in society. Following up on this impulse, the Constitution recognizes both the freedom
of religion as an individual right (Article 25), as well as the right of religious denominations to manage their
own affairs in matters of religion (Article 26). The second impulse, on the other hand, recognises that while
community can be a source of solidarity at the best of times, it can also be a terrain of oppression and exclusion.

The Constitution, therefore, expressly provides for the possibility that there may be times when members of
religious and cultural communities may need to be protected from authoritarian and oppressive social practices.
Thus, both Articles 25 and 26 are subject to public order, morality, and health; and further, Article 25 is also
subject to other fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, and to the state’s power to bring in social
reform laws.

Over the years, the Supreme Court has attempted to strike the balance by carving out a jurisprudence that
virtually allows it to sit in theological judgment over different practices. It has done this by recognizing that it is
only those practices that are “essential” to religion that enjoy constitutional protection. Any other ritual is seen
as secular and amenable to the state's interference. The legislature does not efface a religion altogether, by doing
away with its basic or essential doctrines or practices. Essential religious practices test puts its faith in practices
that bear a very intense and proximate connection to the basic tenants of religion, or are rather integral to the


religion, and any activity would be redundancy if it does not bear such a close connection with the religion
(including practices which may be superstitious) and that may be deemed extraneous. By following this
principle, the concept of social reforms was inherited by the Indian Constitution under Article 25(2)(b) without
impairing the freedom of religion.

questions.stimulus:
VI. According to Section 2(d) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, “when, at the desire of the promisor, the
promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to
do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the
promise.” In the following definition, a promisor is the party that performs a promise and a promisee is the
party to which a promise is made.

Essential elements of consideration:

1. The consideration must move at the desire of the promisor – The definition of consideration under the
Indian Contract Act, 1872, starts with “when, at the desire of the promisor....”, which clearly specifies that any
act or abstinence or promise by the promisee should act at the desire of the promisor. It means that any act or
abstinence done voluntarily or without the desire of the promisor is not a valid consideration in the eyes of the
law.
2. The consideration may move from the promisee to any other person or a third party – As long as there
is no objection by the promisor, the consideration may move to any other person or proceed from any other
person than the promisee. In simple words, it states that it is not a mandate that only the promisee should grant
the consideration; it can also be provided by any other person. The doctrine of privity of consideration is, thus,
not applicable in India.

3. The consideration must not be unlawful – It's very obvious that any act, abstinence or promise made that is
considered illegal in the eyes of the law is not a valid consideration. Also, if there is an involvement of any
injury to a person or property of another person or is immoral in nature, it makes the consideration invalid under
the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Such considerations make the contract void. For example, if you promise a
person to pay Rs. 10,000 for selling drugs at his workplace, such consideration will not be valid.
4. The consideration must not be physically impossible – A consideration that is not physically possible to be
performed or carried out is considered invalid. A decision should always be something that is capable of being


performed or carried out. For example, X makes a promise to Z to pay Rs. 1,00,000 if Z runs 100 km in 1
minute. Here, it is impossible to perform the said task. Thus, such considerations that are physically impossible
to perform are deemed invalid.

5. The consideration may not be adequate – While entering into a contract, consideration is something that is
to be mutually decided by the parties to that contract. When the question of adequacy of consideration arises
while enforcing the contract, the court is not concerned with the adequacy of consideration in it. In simple
words, the court has nothing to do with the question of whether the consideration in the contract is adequate or
not.

questions.stimulus:
VI. According to Section 2(d) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, “when, at the desire of the promisor, the
promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to
do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the
promise.” In the following definition, a promisor is the party that performs a promise and a promisee is the
party to which a promise is made.

Essential elements of consideration:

1. The consideration must move at the desire of the promisor – The definition of consideration under the
Indian Contract Act, 1872, starts with “when, at the desire of the promisor....”, which clearly specifies that any
act or abstinence or promise by the promisee should act at the desire of the promisor. It means that any act or
abstinence done voluntarily or without the desire of the promisor is not a valid consideration in the eyes of the
law.
2. The consideration may move from the promisee to any other person or a third party – As long as there
is no objection by the promisor, the consideration may move to any other person or proceed from any other
person than the promisee. In simple words, it states that it is not a mandate that only the promisee should grant
the consideration; it can also be provided by any other person. The doctrine of privity of consideration is, thus,
not applicable in India.

3. The consideration must not be unlawful – It's very obvious that any act, abstinence or promise made that is
considered illegal in the eyes of the law is not a valid consideration. Also, if there is an involvement of any
injury to a person or property of another person or is immoral in nature, it makes the consideration invalid under
the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Such considerations make the contract void. For example, if you promise a
person to pay Rs. 10,000 for selling drugs at his workplace, such consideration will not be valid.
4. The consideration must not be physically impossible – A consideration that is not physically possible to be
performed or carried out is considered invalid. A decision should always be something that is capable of being


performed or carried out. For example, X makes a promise to Z to pay Rs. 1,00,000 if Z runs 100 km in 1
minute. Here, it is impossible to perform the said task. Thus, such considerations that are physically impossible
to perform are deemed invalid.

to be mutually decided by the parties to that contract. When the question of adequacy of consideration arises
while enforcing the contract, the court is not concerned with the adequacy of consideration in it. In simple
words, the court has nothing to do with the question of whether the consideration in the contract is adequate or
not.

infringement.

copyrighted works that would otherwise be prohibited, fostering growth and creativity. The UK Copyright Act
of 1911 was the first to explicitly recognize fair dealing, providing limitations related to non-commercial
research, private study, criticism, review, and news reporting.

Copyright law. This section incorporates defences for fair dealing, such as for research, private study, criticism,
review, and reporting current events. The Copyright Amendment Act, 2012, expanded fair use to include
cinematograph films and musical works.
Fair dealing is not precisely defined in the Act but is a legal doctrine allowing limited use without permission.

the copyrighted work, the amount used, and the effect on the potential market for the work.

teaching, scholarship, or research. The statute outlines four factors to determine fair use: the purpose and
character of use, the nature of the copyrighted work, the amount used, and the effect on the potential market for
the work.

These factors collectively guide courts in deciding whether a particular use qualifies as fair dealing or fair use.
While fair use allows for transformative uses, the impact on the market remains a crucial consideration.

legally protected intellectual property landscape.

I. India is a land of contradictions. It is a place where ancient traditions and modern innovations coexist side by
side. The country's heritage is a source of pride for its citizens, but it is also a burden that weighs heavily on the
shoulders of those who seek to embrace modernity. India's cultural heritage is rich and diverse. It is home to


countless temples, monuments, and artifacts that date back thousands of years. Many of these treasures are still
in use today, serving as places of worship, pilgrimage, and tourism. At the same time, India is also a rapidly
developing nation. Its cities are bustling with activity, its economy is growing at an unprecedented pace, and its
people are becoming more cosmopolitan and global in their outlook.

The challenge facing India today is how to balance its rich cultural heritage with the demands of modernity.
How can the country preserve its traditions and customs while also embracing the latest technologies and
innovations? One solution is to look to the past for inspiration. Many of India's ancient traditions are still
relevant today, and can provide valuable insights into how to live a fulfilling and meaningful life. For example,
the practice of yoga, which dates back thousands of years, has become a global phenomenon in recent years,
with millions of people around the world practicing it as a way to stay fit, reduce stress, and enhance their
overall well-being.

Similarly, India's cuisine, which is renowned for its rich flavors and spices, has also undergone a modern
transformation. While traditional dishes like biryani and dosa remain popular, new fusion cuisines have
emerged that combine Indian flavors with international cooking styles, creating a unique culinary experience
that appeals to a global audience. Another way to balance tradition and modernity is to embrace technology
while preserving cultural values. For example, India's digital revolution has opened up new opportunities for
education, healthcare, and entrepreneurship, while also preserving traditional knowledge and practices. The rise
of e-learning platforms has made it easier for people to access education and training, while telemedicine has
made healthcare more accessible to those in remote areas.
Finally, India can also look to other countries for inspiration on how to balance tradition and modernity.
Countries like Japan and South Korea have successfully integrated their rich cultural heritage with modern
technologies and innovations, creating a unique blend of ancient and modern that is both inspiring and relevant.
In conclusion, India's rich cultural heritage is a source of pride and inspiration, but it must also evolve to meet
the demands of the modern world. By embracing the latest technologies and innovations, while also preserving
traditional customs and values, India can create a unique blend of ancient and modern that will inspire
generations to come.

there are serious concerns that this reduction will have a negative impact on the Army's operational capabilities.

The Indian Army is responsible for defending India’s borders and maintaining internal security. It is also
involved in a range of other tasks, including counter-insurgency operations, disaster relief, and peacekeeping
missions. In order to carry out these tasks effectively, the Army needs to have a certain level of manpower.

has been trying to upgrade its equipment and weapons systems in order to keep pace with the changing security
environment. However, the process of modernisation requires a significant amount of funds and resources, as
well as trained personnel to operate and maintain the new equipment. With fewer soldiers, the Army will find it
difficult to implement its modernisation plans.
Another concern is that the reduction in manpower will lead to an increase in the stress levels of soldiers. The
Army is already facing a high rate of attrition due to a number of factors, including prolonged deployments,
lack of adequate rest and recreation facilities, and inadequate compensation. With fewer soldiers, the workload
on the remaining soldiers is likely to increase, leading to higher stress levels and increased risk of burnout.

Moreover, the reduction in manpower will impact the Army's ability to maintain its current level of operational
readiness. The Army needs to be prepared for any contingency at all times, which requires a certain level of
operational readiness. With fewer soldiers, the Army may find it difficult to maintain this level of readiness,
which could have serious implications for national security.

It is important to note that the reduction in manpower is not the only challenge facing the Army. The Army is
also facing a shortage of officers, particularly at the junior level. This shortage is due to a number of factors,
including the high rate of attrition, inadequate compensation, and the perception that the Army is not a viable
career option for young people.

In order to address these challenges, the Army needs to take a number of steps. First, it needs to ensure that the
reduction in manpower does not impact its operational capabilities. This may require a re-evaluation of the
Army's current structure and deployment patterns. Second, it needs to address the shortage of officers,
particularly at the junior level. This may require a review of the compensation and benefits package for officers,
as well as efforts to improve the perception of the Army as a viable career option.
